title: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) of the Eyelid
summary: The most common malignant eyelid tumor worldwide, BCC is a slow-growing but locally invasive neoplasm derived from the basal layer of the epidermis. This guide provides a comprehensive clinical roadmap from molecular pathogenesis to advanced Mohs surgical techniques.

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC) accounts for approximately 90% of all malignant eyelid tumors. While it rarely metastasizes (less than 0.1%), it is characterized by significant local destruction and invasion if left untreated. It arises from the pluripotential cells in the basal layer of the epidermis and is particularly common in the periocular region due to chronic ultraviolet (UV) exposure.

sections.title: Etiology & Risk Factors
content: UVB Exposure: Primary environmental driver (DNA damage).
Phenotype: Fitzpatrick Type I & II (fair skin, blue eyes, red hair).
Genetics: PTCH1 gene mutations (Hedgehog signaling pathway).
Syndromes: Gorlin-Goltz (Basal Cell Nevus Syndrome), Bazex, Xeroderma Pigmentosum.
Previous Radiation: History of radiotherapy for other conditions.
Immunosuppression: Post-transplant or HIV patients.

branches: PTCH1 Mutation: Loss of inhibition on SMO
SMO Activation: Triggers GLI transcription factors
GLI1/GLI2: Upregulate genes for cell proliferation/survival
TP53 Mutations: Found in 50% of sporadic cases
Peripheral Palisading: Typical histopathologic cell arrangement

sections.title: Ocular Examination Findings
content: Pearly Border: Rolled, translucent edges.
Telangiectasia: Fine, branching vessels on the surface.
Madarosis: Localized loss of eyelashes (highly suspicious).
Meibomian Gland Distortion: Notched lid margin.
Fixation: Tumor attachment to underlying periosteum.
Canthal Involvement: Check for orbital extension/motility.

sections.title: Red Flags: High-Risk Features
content: Medial Canthal Location: Higher risk of deep orbital invasion.
Morpheaform/Sclerosing Subtype: Invisible lateral spread.
Recurrent Lesions: Higher risk of perineural invasion.
Perineural Invasion: Patient reports pain or paresthesia.
Tumor Size >20mm: Increased risk of recurrence.
Immunocompromised State: Rapid growth and multiple lesions.

rows: Faster growth, more scaling, lacks pearly border
Yellowish hue, associated with blepharitis, pagetoid spread
Central keratin plug, rapid onset then regression
Lack of characteristic BCC features, rapid growth

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Biopsy
content: 1. Clinical Photography for documentation.
2. Incisional Biopsy (Punch or Shave): For large or suspicious lesions.
3. Histopathology: Look for peripheral palisading & retraction artifact.
4. Imaging (CT/MRI): Only if orbital or bone invasion is suspected.
5. Lymph Node Palpation: Check preauricular and submandibular nodes.

content.explanation: Pearly nodules, Pink color, Peripheral palisading (path), Persistent ulcer, and Pre-cancerous UV exposure.

rows: Tumor > 20mm OR involving tarsal plate/lid margin
Tumor involving full thickness eyelid OR ocular structures
Tumor involving orbit, sinuses, or brain

sections.title: Management & Treatment Protocols
content: Step 1: Surgical Excision with Frozen Section: 3-4mm clear margins standard.
Step 2: Mohs Micrographic Surgery (MMS): Gold standard for medial canthal or morpheaform types.
Step 3: Reconstruction: Direct closure, Tenzel flap, or Hughes tarsoconjunctival flap.
Step 4: Non-Surgical (Small/Superficial): Imiquimod 5% cream or Cryotherapy.
Step 5: Advanced/Metastatic Case: Vismodegib (Hedgehog inhibitor) or Radiotherapy.

sections.title: Surgical Reconstruction Pearls
content: Primary Closure: Possible for <33% lid defect.
Tenzel Semicircular Flap: Best for 33-50% moderate defects.
Hughes Flap: For large (>50%) lower lid defects using upper lid tarsus.
Mustardé Flap: Large cheek rotation flap for total lower lid loss.
Cutler-Beard Flap: Full thickness upper lid reconstruction.

sections.title: Systemic Hedgehog Inhibitors
content: Drug Name: Vismodegib (Erivedge) or Sonidegib.
Indication: Metastatic BCC or locally advanced BCC not amenable to surgery.
Mechanism: SMO (Smoothened) protein antagonist.
Common Side Effects: Muscle cramps (71%), alopecia (61%), dysgeusia (loss of taste).
Pregnancy Warning: Category X (highly teratogenic).

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Recurrence Rate: <5% with Mohs; higher with standard excision.
Canalicular Involvement: Requires intubation or dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR).
Orbital Invasion: May necessitate orbital exenteration in rare cases.
Cicatricial Ectropion: Potential post-operative complication.
Metastasis: Extremely rare, usually to regional lymph nodes or lungs.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for the Board Exam
content: Medial canthal BCCs have 'silent' deep invasion along the periosteum.
A 'recurrent chalazion' is SCC or Sebaceous Carcinoma until proven otherwise (BCC is less likely to mimic a chalazion).
Cryotherapy is contraindicated for morpheaform BCC.
In Gorlin Syndrome, lesions appear at a young age; avoid radiation due to risk of secondary tumors.
